posts.name: Puru Saxena
posts.text:
The AI selloff is not about demand evaporating. It is about cash flow, financing cost and how long the market is willing to wait for the returns.

Demand signals remain extremely strong.

SK hynix just reported Q3 revenue of 104.6 trillion won (+328% YoY) and operating profit of 83.3 trillion won with an ~80% margin. Management said DRAM and HBM volumes are effectively sold out through 2029, customer HBM requests are roughly double what they can supply, and they expect the supply shortage to persist through 2030. Long-term agreements already cover more than half of 2027–2028 capacity with 14 major customers. That is not a demand problem.⁠

Anthropic’s S-1 shows the unit economics at the model layer improving sharply. Revenue per dollar of compute and infrastructure expense rose from $0.40 in Q1 2025 to $2.08 in Q2 2026 - a 5.2× improvement in five quarters. Compute costs fell from 251% of revenue to 48%. The company generated its first quarterly operating profit. Revenue grew 1,368% YoY while compute expense rose only ~300%. Efficiency is rising, not collapsing.⁠

GPU rental prices have turned higher again. B200 on-demand rates rose more than 20% in a month in some indices; H100 and H200 also firmed. Tightness in the spot and short-term rental market is consistent with the hyperscalers’ own comments that they still cannot meet all the demand they see.⁠

On the supply side the hyperscalers themselves are not signalling a slowdown. Amazon maintained ~$220 billion 2026 cash capex and said it will spend “meaningfully more” in 2027, with Andy Jassy noting that even at these levels demand will still exceed capacity. Alphabet kept its $195–205 billion 2026 range and said 2027 capex will rise significantly. Meta raised the bottom of its range. These are the companies closest to the demand. They are still leaving demand on the table and planning higher spend next year.⁠

What the market is reacting to is the cash flow and financing picture.

In Q3, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta reported negative free cash flow. Theses companies are now funding the gap with a combination of operating cash, new debt and equity issuance. Amazon alone raised substantial long-term debt in the quarter. Combined 2026 capex guidance across the major hyperscalers is now in the $700+ billion range.⁠

This is the classic tension Philip Fisher described in Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits: exceptional companies will temporarily depress free cash flow and reported earnings when they invest heavily in capacity that expands long-term earning power. The market often treats the near-term cash burn as a problem rather than the necessary cost of building the next phase of growth. Fisher’s view was that investors who focus on the long-range profit outlook and are willing to look through the temporary expense should benefit when the results arrive.

The valuation backdrop is also different from prior bubbles. The NASDAQ Composite’s trailing PE is in the high-20s today versus roughly 190× at the March 2000 peak. The multiple then was several times higher. This is not a pure multiple-expansion story running on narratives alone.

The risks are there and they are mostly about financing and timing, not about whether the underlying demand for AI compute exists:

- How long free cash flow stays under pressure and how expensive or available the external capital becomes.
- Whether power, memory and data-centre delivery constraints stretch the payback further than expected.
- Whether core businesses (search, advertising, traditional cloud) slow enough to offset the AI-driven growth in the near term.

Nonetheless the primary evidence from the companies building the capacity (hyperscalers), the companies supplying the critical components (memory) and the companies delivering the models (Anthropic and others) points to demand that continues to exceed available supply. The stocks have sold off because investors are now focused on the cash flow gap and the cost of bridging it, not because

The professors went quiet.

posts.name: Andy Constan
posts.text:
I have somewhat different view than most having cut my options teeth on a dispersion book during the tech bubble.  

The index vol short half of the short correlation trade was always a choice in terms of its sizing.  Back then IV/RV premium was pretty narrow unlike today so every unit of Vega sold in index was managed carefully.  Being short index vol was a coin flip sort of trade.   The sizing ranged from Vega neutral to single stock book (which collected theta) to theta neutral which was Vega long. 

The drop in implied correlation makes the trade less attractive.  But given the level of implied on index the notable risk isn't selling index vol to low its buying single name vol way way too high.  The root causes of that single name vol levels are numerous including speculative demand and the dispersion trader competing to buy elevated single name vol.  the seller is absent and gets a sweet risk premium when providing any liquidity. The risk the dispersionis at most risk to is a single name vol  collapse.  Perhaps a large equity drawdown would also be a negative single name vol event but that seems pretty unlikely.  So then it comes down to hedging index level and sizing.

posts.name: GonzalesJ
posts.text:
Brent just printed $118 and the 10-year Treasury yield is at 4.94%. That relationship used to run the other way .

@robin_j_brooks is correct in this analysis. This is a regime shift, not a blip.

For most of 2026, oil up meant yields up. Inflation expectations fed straight into the long end. That link is now broken. The 20-day correlation between Brent and the 10Y has collapsed to its lowest since late 2024.

The reason is Europe. The French 10-year is at 4.96%, the highest since 2002. The spread over German Bunds has widened to 159bp, the widest since 2011. French debt-to-GDP is 117%, versus 90% at the last crisis peak.

Bessent confirmed this week that capital is leaving "concerning" jurisdictions and flowing into Treasuries as a safe haven. The US is catching a bid because the alternative is worse.

This is not a resolution of the fiscal problem. Net interest is still above $1 trillion. The term premium is being temporarily suppressed by a flight to quality, not by better US math.

If Europe stabilizes, the bid fades. If Europe cracks, the bid deepens.

quoted.text:
Chamath: The AI Boom Has a Borrowing Problem

“The entire United States economy is levered to the AI complex.

So very narrowly, we're talking about seven or eight companies that set the tone for the entire country. And whether we like it or not, that is where we are.

Why do I say that? The most important companies in the world are in a massive spending binge, right?

These were highly profitable, highly cash accretive, highly cash flow generative businesses that have said, ‘We're going to put the foot down on spending because we believe in what's coming into the future.’ That's what drives GDP and it's what drives growth.

Now, as they do that though, they deplete their cash and they have to raise debt.

The AI complex now owes $340-400 billion to the market. And you'd say, ‘Okay, why is that important?’

The problem is this: These companies are raising so much money it starts to crowd out the capital markets.

And the most important part of the capital market that it starts to crowd out, is the appetite for government treasuries.

And what you can see here is that when you look at these AI firms, the amount of money that they need to raise through the end of '27, it's 30% of all of what the Treasury's about to issue in that same period.

So, whether we like it or not, they are going to start competing for demand.”
